questions.stem: An electronic act will use audio-video communication. What must participants be told before the act?
options: That the electronic notarization will be recorded
That the recording is optional for every act
That the journal replaces the recording
That the notary guarantees document enforceability
questions.explanation: The electronic notary must inform all participating persons that the act will be electronically recorded.
feedback: Correct. Advance recording notice is required.
Recording is required for this procedure.
The recording is additional to the journal entry.
The ceremony does not guarantee enforceability.

questions.stem: An electronic audio-video session ends without completion of the act. How does the statutory recording retention rule apply?
options: Delete it immediately because no seal was applied
Keep the recording at least seven years even if the act was not completed
Keep it only until midnight
Let the customer choose a one-day period
questions.explanation: The statute requires at least seven years of recording retention regardless of completion.
feedback: Noncompletion does not remove this retention duty.
Correct. The statute expressly includes uncompleted acts.
Midnight is too early.
Customer preference does not shorten the statutory period.

questions.stem: An electronic notary personally knows the remote signer. What should the recording include about that identification?
options: Only the signer's first name
Only a private ID number
How the notary knows the person and how long
A claim that no identification method was used
questions.explanation: When personal knowledge is used, the recording must explain the relationship and its duration.
feedback: A first name does not provide the required explanation.
ID numbers do not explain personal knowledge.
Correct. Record how and how long the notary has known the signer.
The notary must truthfully identify the method used.

questions.stem: A platform proposes replacing live electronic notarization with separate prerecorded messages. What does the Act require?
options: Any video content
Only a silent webcam image
A later telephone call
Simultaneous two-way sight and speech with real-time transmission
questions.explanation: Electronic audio-video communication must permit simultaneous seeing and speaking and use real-time transmission.
feedback: Generic video does not ensure live interaction.
Silent video cannot provide the required two-way speech.
A later call does not create the required session.
Correct. Live simultaneous communication is required.

questions.stem: An electronic signer exits the identity workflow before completing verification. What must happen on return?
options: Restart identity verification from the beginning
Resume at the final question automatically
Skip credential analysis
Ask the notary to guess the result
questions.explanation: Rule 176.825(c) requires restarting identity verification after exiting the workflow before completion.
feedback: Correct. Restart the identity process.
The rule does not authorize automatic continuation.
Leaving does not eliminate required analysis.
A guess does not establish identity.

questions.stem: An unknown electronic signer remotely presents a credential. What does the statutory non-personal-knowledge route require?
options: Only a photograph of any card
Remote credential presentation, credential analysis and dynamic knowledge-based authentication
Only a verbal name
Only the notary's employer approval
questions.explanation: Section 6A-103(b)(2) requires all three components for the described electronic identity route.
feedback: A photograph alone omits required components.
Correct. Presentation, analysis and dynamic KBA are required.
A verbal name alone is insufficient.
Employer approval does not replace identity verification.

questions.stem: A remote electronic credential passes automated analysis, but the person on camera clearly differs from the photograph. What responsibility remains?
options: The software result replaces all observation
The vendor may ignore the mismatch
The notary must visually compare the credential and principal
The journal fee can cure the problem
questions.explanation: Rule 176.835 requires a process permitting the notary's real-time visual comparison.
feedback: Automated analysis does not eliminate comparison.
A mismatch cannot simply be disregarded.
Correct. The notary must make the required comparison.
Fees do not establish identity.

questions.stem: A dynamic knowledge-based identity quiz offers only three questions. What minimum is required by Rule 176.835(c)?
options: One question
Two questions
Four questions
At least five questions
questions.explanation: The identity quiz must contain at least five questions about personal history or identity.
feedback: One question is below the minimum.
Two questions are below the minimum.
Four questions are below the minimum.
Correct. The minimum is five questions.

questions.stem: A knowledge-based identity quiz gives each question only two answer choices. What minimum applies?
options: At least five possible answers per question
Exactly two choices
No answer choices
Only a yes/no response
questions.explanation: Each dynamic knowledge-based question must have at least five possible answer choices.
feedback: Correct. The rule requires at least five choices.
Two choices do not meet the rule.
The assessment requires answer choices.
A yes/no format does not meet the minimum.

questions.stem: A principal answers 60% of the dynamic identity quiz correctly. What passing standard applies?
options: At least 80%
100% in every case
The notary chooses afterward
questions.explanation: At least 80% of the dynamic KBA questions must be answered correctly.
feedback: 50% is below the required threshold.
Correct. The standard is at least 80%.
The rule specifies 80%, not universal perfection.
The notary cannot select a different threshold afterward.

questions.stem: A provider gives a principal ten minutes to complete the required dynamic identity quiz. What rule timing applies?
options: No timing requirement
Thirty minutes
All questions answered within two minutes
Three hours of instructional time
questions.explanation: The dynamic KBA questions must be answered within two minutes.
feedback: The rule specifies a limit.
Thirty minutes exceeds the specified limit.
Correct. The identity quiz has a two-minute limit.
Course instruction time is a different specification.

questions.stem: A principal fails the first dynamic KBA attempt and seeks an immediate retry. What does the rule allow?
options: Unlimited retries with identical questions
No retry ever
Three retries every hour
One retake within 24 hours with required question replacement
questions.explanation: The rule allows one retake within 24 hours and requires at least 40% of prior questions to be replaced.
feedback: The rule limits retries and requires changed questions.
One retake is permitted.
The rule does not authorize three hourly retries.
Correct. Follow both the attempt and replacement conditions.

questions.stem: After a second failed KBA attempt, the same electronic notary is asked to begin a third attempt immediately. What applies?
options: No retry with that notary within 24 hours of the second failure
A mandatory third immediate attempt
The notary may read the answers aloud
The signer may pay to waive the restriction
questions.explanation: A second failure bars retry with the same electronic notary within 24 hours of that failure.
feedback: Correct. The waiting rule applies to the same notary.
The rule does not require an immediate third attempt.
The notary must not see or record the KBA questions or answers.
Payment cannot waive identity standards.

questions.stem: A remote signer asks the notary to display and record the KBA answers for coaching. What does Rule 176.835 require?
options: The notary must coach every answer
The notary must not be able to see or record the questions or answers
The answers must be entered in the journal
The employer may answer for the signer
questions.explanation: The notary must not be able to see or record the dynamic KBA questions or answers.
feedback: Coaching conflicts with the independent identity assessment.
Correct. The assessment must protect questions and answers from the notary.
The answers do not belong in the journal.
The signer must complete the identity assessment.

questions.stem: An electronic seal is attached as an editable image with no protection against later document changes. What is required?
options: Only attractive artwork
Only the vendor's logo
Independent verification and tamper-evident association with the electronic certificate
A printed business card
questions.explanation: Electronic signatures and seals must be independently verifiable and associated in a tamper-evident manner.
feedback: Appearance does not establish security.
A logo does not create verifiability.
Correct. Required security must reveal subsequent changes.
A business card does not secure the electronic record.

questions.stem: A coworker requests the electronic-seal password to cover an absent notary's appointments. What should happen?
options: Share it if the coworker is trained
Share it only with supervisors
Share it for low-value documents
Keep access under the commissioned notary's exclusive control
questions.explanation: The electronic signature and seal must remain under the notary's exclusive control and cannot be used by another person.
feedback: Training does not authorize use of another notary's seal.
Supervisory rank does not confer access authority.
Document value does not remove exclusive control.
Correct. The notary must protect the access information.

questions.stem: An electronic notary discovers seal credentials were compromised. What immediate statutory reporting deadline applies?
options: No later than the next business day to law enforcement, vendor and Secretary
At the next commission renewal
Within three years
Only if the client complains
questions.explanation: Section 3-101(d)(2) requires notice to the listed recipients no later than the next business day.
feedback: Correct. Notify all three specified recipients promptly.
Renewal can be far too late.
Three years exceeds the deadline.
Discovery triggers the duty.

questions.stem: A paper remote session loses its audio-video link during signing. What does Rule 176.720 require?
options: Finish by voice call only
Restart the remote act from the beginning, including identity confirmation
Assume the last image is enough
Backdate a certificate after a later email
questions.explanation: The rule requires restarting when the link breaks, a participant exits or the process is compromised.
feedback: A voice-only finish does not satisfy the restart rule.
Correct. Restart the full procedure.
A frozen image cannot supply the required continuing session.
A later email does not cure the interrupted ceremony.

questions.stem: A paper remote signer sends only the signature page two days after signing. What statutory transmission requirement was missed?
options: Only the signature page within a month
Only a verbal description
A legible copy of the entire signed document by no later than the next day
A blank document before signing
questions.explanation: Section 6-102.5(c)(1) requires the entire legible signed document to be sent directly to the notary no later than the next day.
feedback: The rule requires the entire document and a shorter deadline.
A description does not transmit the signed document.
Correct. Both completeness and timing matter.
A blank document does not establish the completed remote instrument.

questions.stem: A notary receives the legible copy following a compliant paper remote signing. What return step does §6-102.5(c)(2) require?
options: Keep the copy indefinitely without responding
Let the employer sign as the notary
Return an unsigned receipt only
Sign the transmitted copy as witness and send it back within 24 hours after receipt
questions.explanation: The notary must sign the transmitted copy and return it through the permitted means within 24 hours of receipt.
feedback: The statute requires timely return.
An employer cannot sign the notary's name.
An unsigned receipt does not perform the required return step.
Correct. Follow the signature and 24-hour return requirement.

questions.stem: A remote paper certificate omits any mention of audio-video technology. What does Rule 176.730 require?
options: A statement substantially indicating use of audio-video technology
Only a handwritten smile
Only the vendor's invoice number
No certificate for remote paper acts
questions.explanation: The remote-paper certificate must contain the prescribed or substantially similar audio-video statement.
feedback: Correct. The certificate must disclose the remote technology.
A symbol does not supply the required statement.
An invoice number does not state the remote method.
Remote acts still require a certificate.

cards.title: Final examination structure
cards.front: What makes the provider final compliant?
cards.rule: The final draws 50 randomized questions from a bank of at least 100. At most half may be true-or-false.
cards.boundary: A minimum 85% score is required.
cards.mixup: A short practice quiz is not certified provider completion.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.235(c)(3)-(4)

cards.title: Failed final progression
cards.front: What changes after repeated final failures?
cards.rule: Retesting uses different questions through the provider. Three unsuccessful examinations constitute course failure.
cards.boundary: The provider's compliant retesting arrangements still apply.
cards.mixup: A first failure and three failures have different consequences.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.235(c)(4)-(5)

cards.title: Renewal education exception
cards.front: Who must check the 2025 renewal exemption?
cards.rule: Specified qualifying attorneys, judges and employees may seek the renewal education/exam exemption through the prescribed signed statement and current-law reading.
cards.boundary: The exemption is limited to qualifying renewals.
cards.mixup: Employment in a law office does not create a blanket first-application exemption.
cards.source: Illinois Register, January 10, 2025, adopted notary amendments — §176.205(e)

cards.title: Course scope
cards.front: Why inspect a course's scope disclosure?
cards.rule: A certified provider may offer traditional-only education and disclose that it does not qualify the student for electronic authority.
cards.boundary: Electronic applicants must satisfy the applicable educational scope.
cards.mixup: Certified traditional completion does not automatically establish electronic qualification.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.215(n)

cards.title: Resident filing route
cards.front: How do Illinois residents normally file?
cards.rule: Residents use the official online application with the required unexpired Illinois ID, completion certificate and bond documents.
cards.boundary: An approved hardship exception permits a paper route. Qualifying nonresidents use the paper application.
cards.mixup: A preferred filing method does not replace the official route.
cards.source: Illinois online notary application instructions — Online application instructions

cards.title: Authority starts with appointment
cards.front: What must be ready before a first notarization?
cards.rule: The applicant needs an effective state commission and the required official seal after approval.
cards.boundary: A bond purchase and a course certificate are prerequisites, not appointment.
cards.mixup: A supplies order does not start the commission term.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §§176.110,176.310,176.510

cards.title: Renewal-window discrepancy
cards.front: How should a learner use the competing renewal windows?
cards.rule: The online instructions advertise 90 days before expiration. Published Rule 176.350 says 60 days. Confirm the current filing opportunity through the official portal or office.
cards.boundary: Expiration still ends authority without a grace period.
cards.mixup: The discrepancy does not authorize post-expiration acts.
cards.source: Illinois online notary application instructions — Online renewal instructions; §176.350

cards.title: Bond levels
cards.front: How do ordinary and remote bonds relate?
cards.rule: The ordinary bond is $5,000. Remote/electronic work requires the additional $25,000 coverage or qualifying combined $30,000 bond.
cards.boundary: Coverage must match the intended work and application.
cards.mixup: A bond is financial protection, not permission to act before commissioning.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.340

cards.title: Three identity paths
cards.front: What are the ordinary Illinois identity routes?
cards.rule: Use genuine personal knowledge, the oath or affirmation of a credible witness personally known to the notary, or qualifying current documentary ID.
cards.boundary: The ordinary statutory witness language requires the notary's personal knowledge of the witness.
cards.mixup: An unsworn introduction is not a credible-witness oath.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-102(d)

cards.title: Current document standard
cards.front: Which elements must documentary identification combine?
cards.rule: The credential must be valid at the act, issued by a qualifying state/federal agency or consulate, and bear the person's facial photograph and signature.
cards.boundary: The notary still determines that the appearing person is the correct individual.
cards.mixup: A photograph alone does not satisfy the documentary route.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-102(d)(3)

cards.title: Appearance remains separate
cards.front: Why does a license copy not solve an absent-signer request?
cards.rule: Identity evidence supports identifying a person who appears for the act. Appearance must occur in person or through a fully lawful remote procedure.
cards.boundary: A courier holding the absent person's ID does not create that person's appearance.
cards.mixup: Documents and people satisfy different parts of the procedure.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §§6-102,6-102.5

cards.title: Directed signature participants
cards.front: Who participates when physical inability prevents signing?
cards.rule: Under Rule 176.610, the principal directs a person other than the notary to sign. Both principal and directed signer appear and are identified.
cards.boundary: The specified or substantially similar direction statement goes near the signature.
cards.mixup: The assistant's presence alone does not replace the principal.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.610

cards.title: Blind signer's acknowledgment
cards.front: What additional step precedes this acknowledgment?
cards.rule: The notary reads the instrument to the blind signer before taking the acknowledgment.
cards.boundary: This is an express Illinois acknowledgment requirement.
cards.mixup: A waiver of the reading does not replace the statutory step.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(e)

cards.title: Language comprehension
cards.front: What must an English-nonunderstanding signer receive before acknowledgment?
cards.rule: The instrument's nature and effect must be translated into a language the signer understands.
cards.boundary: Identity and the actual acknowledgment remain required.
cards.mixup: An English name does not establish understanding of the instrument.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(f)

cards.title: Witness solemnity
cards.front: What turns a witness introduction into the statutory identity procedure?
cards.rule: The qualifying credible witness identifies the person upon oath or affirmation.
cards.boundary: For the ordinary route the witness is personally known to the notary.
cards.mixup: A business title or friendly text does not administer an oath.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-102(d)(2)

cards.title: Refusal discretion
cards.front: Does a current ID compel every act?
cards.rule: Illinois allows a notary or electronic notary to refuse an act without further explanation.
cards.boundary: A valid credential does not remove other requirements or refusal discretion.
cards.mixup: A manager's demand does not become the notary's identity judgment.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-102(e)

cards.title: Acknowledging prior execution
cards.front: What can be declared about an earlier signature?
cards.rule: An identified signer may appear and acknowledge an already executed signature as their own.
cards.boundary: The acknowledgment still requires the signer's appearance and declaration.
cards.mixup: The acknowledgment note does not authorize after-the-fact signature witnessing.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-105(a), practice note

cards.title: Verification ceremony
cards.front: What actions support an Illinois verification?
cards.rule: The signer appears, signs before the notary and swears or affirms that the statement is true.
cards.boundary: Certificate wording records the ceremony actually performed.
cards.mixup: A printed jurat does not itself administer an oath.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-105(c), practice note

cards.title: Solemn affirmation
cards.front: How can a signer avoid religious oath wording?
cards.rule: The signer may make a solemn affirmation for verification. Illinois recognizes oath and affirmation.
cards.boundary: The truth declaration must actually occur.
cards.mixup: Affirmation is not an informal waiver of truthfulness.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-101(c)

cards.title: Representative declaration
cards.front: What does representative acknowledgment add?
cards.rule: The person declares proper authority and execution as the act of the represented person or entity.
cards.boundary: The appearing representative must be identified.
cards.mixup: The notary is not guaranteeing the entity's performance.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-101(b),(d)

cards.title: Witnessed signing
cards.front: What distinguishes the event recorded by signature witnessing?
cards.rule: The identified person appears and signs before the notary. The handbook states that an oath is not necessary for this form.
cards.boundary: The certificate must accurately reflect the observed act.
cards.mixup: An earlier unobserved signature does not become witnessed through a stamp.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-105(d), practice note

cards.title: Certificate essentials
cards.front: Which facts anchor an ordinary certificate?
cards.rule: The certificate is signed and dated by the notary, identifies the act's jurisdiction and carries the official seal.
cards.boundary: The actual performed act determines truthful certificate facts.
cards.mixup: Drafting date and destination county do not set the notarization date or venue.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-103(a)

cards.title: Permanent certificate connection
cards.front: How is a separate paper certificate secured?
cards.rule: Use permanent tamper-evident attachment such as staples. Tape, paper clips and binder clips are excluded.
cards.boundary: The certificate belongs to the specific notarized instrument.
cards.mixup: A loose reusable certificate does not satisfy attachment.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.600(c)

cards.title: Readable official signature
cards.front: How should an illegible preferred signature be supported?
cards.rule: The notary adds their legibly printed name immediately adjacent to the handwritten signature.
cards.boundary: Use the commissioned name or initials as required.
cards.mixup: Typing the name alone does not replace the required official signature.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.600(d); §6-104(a)

cards.title: Contemporaneous default
cards.front: When are nonexempt acts entered?
cards.rule: Record each nonexempt notarial act in the journal at the time of notarization.
cards.boundary: Specific law-firm and candidate-document exceptions require their stated facts.
cards.mixup: A busy office schedule does not defer the default duty.
cards.source: Illinois Register, January 10, 2025, adopted notary amendments — §176.900(a),(f)-(h)

cards.title: Law-firm retained copies
cards.front: When may office document copies support the special exception?
cards.rule: A notary employed by an attorney or law firm need not journal employment notarizations if the employer maintains copies of the notarized documents.
cards.boundary: Outside-employment acts do not automatically share the exception.
cards.mixup: The rule is more specific than an ordinary employer's recordkeeping policy.
cards.source: Illinois Register, January 10, 2025, adopted notary amendments — §176.900(f)

cards.title: Law-firm ownership and privilege
cards.front: Which special protections accompany law-firm journals?
cards.rule: A journal solely of notarizations within that employment belongs to the employing attorney or firm. The rule preserves attorney-client privilege against required violation through inspection.
cards.boundary: Apply the provision to its stated employment facts.
cards.mixup: A general employer rule should not erase this specific exception.
cards.source: Illinois Register, January 10, 2025, adopted notary amendments — §176.900(f)

cards.title: Candidate nomination documents
cards.front: Which electoral acts have the journal exception?
cards.rule: Specified nominating petitions, candidacy or nomination petitions and nominating or nomination papers filed by or on behalf of candidates qualify.
cards.boundary: An unrelated commercial contract is outside the listed document types.
cards.mixup: The exception removes the journal entry duty for those acts, not identity or the ceremony.
cards.source: Illinois Register, January 10, 2025, adopted notary amendments — §176.900(g)-(h); §3-107(f)

cards.title: Required entry record
cards.front: What transaction details belong in the entry?
cards.rule: Record principal, relied-on credible witnesses and directed signers, document title/description, date, method, fee and physical locations of notary and principal.
cards.boundary: For journal-entry address the rule means city and state only.
cards.mixup: Capturing extra sensitive identifiers is not a substitute for required fields.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.910(a),(f)

cards.title: Prohibited identifiers
cards.front: Which tempting security details must stay out of the journal?
cards.rule: Do not record government ID numbers, other identifying numbers, biometric identifiers, specified linked personal data or signers' and witnesses' electronic signatures.
cards.boundary: Redact inadvertently recorded prohibited information before lawful public access or copies.
cards.mixup: A commercial template cannot override Illinois privacy limits.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.910(c)-(d)

cards.title: Tangible integrity
cards.front: What protects a paper journal's structure?
cards.rule: Use binding designed to prevent insertion, removal or substitution, with preprinted consecutive page and line/entry numbering.
cards.boundary: Tape and removable clips do not provide compliant binding.
cards.mixup: A stack of loose pages is not a compliant tangible journal.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.920(b)-(d)

cards.title: Retention after last act
cards.front: What is the ordinary tangible-journal retention anchor?
cards.rule: Retain a tangible journal for at least seven years after its final recorded notarial act.
cards.boundary: The Part includes a governmental-employment retention exception.
cards.mixup: Retirement and commission expiration do not by themselves end ordinary retention.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.920(g)-(h)

cards.title: Fees in the record
cards.front: How are free acts and other charges represented?
cards.rule: Indicate no notarial charge with a notation such as zero. Separately itemize any clerical or administrative fees.
cards.boundary: Notarial charges must correspond to the actual act.
cards.mixup: A blank or inflated fee should not misrepresent the transaction.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.910(e)

cards.title: Ordinary custody
cards.front: Who controls a nonexempt ordinary journal?
cards.rule: The notary keeps custody and secure exclusive access during the commission. The ordinary termination rule bars surrender to the employer.
cards.boundary: The special attorney/law-firm provision must be considered where applicable.
cards.mixup: Employer payment alone does not transfer ordinary custody.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.940(a); §3-107(d); §176.900(f)

cards.title: Party and self-signature checks
cards.front: Which personal interests require screening?
cards.rule: Do not notarize your own signature. Do not acknowledge an instrument in which your name appears as a transaction party.
cards.boundary: Corporate capacity does not authorize self-notarization.
cards.mixup: Another stamp impression cannot remove a conflict.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(b); FAQ self-notarization

cards.title: Blank certificate danger
cards.front: Why reject advance-signed certificate forms?
cards.rule: Illinois prohibits affixing the notary's signature to a blank affidavit or acknowledgment form.
cards.boundary: The certificate must evidence a real completed act.
cards.mixup: An employer's convenience does not authorize advance certification.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(c)

cards.title: Signed instrument integrity
cards.front: What must a notary avoid after a document is signed?
cards.rule: Do not change anything in the written instrument after anyone has signed it.
cards.boundary: Completing the notary's own proper certificate is a separate authorized function.
cards.mixup: Finding a typo does not grant authority to edit the signed instrument.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(g)-(h)

cards.title: Document drafting limits
cards.front: Which writing belongs to the ordinary notary role?
cards.rule: The notary may complete the notary certificate. The commission does not authorize preparing legal instruments or filling their blanks.
cards.boundary: The statute preserves its stated attorney-notary provision.
cards.mixup: A customer's waiver does not create legal-drafting authority.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(h)

cards.title: Non-English advertising
cards.front: Which disclosures accompany covered advertising?
cards.rule: The covered nonattorney notary supplies the required conspicuous notice in English and the advertising language, and follows the related fee posting and acknowledgment rules.
cards.boundary: The Act has specified qualifications and exceptions that must be checked.
cards.mixup: Translating a title to imply attorney status does not expand authority.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §3-103(a)-(c-5)

cards.title: Acknowledgment record retention
cards.front: How long are covered customer nonattorney acknowledgments kept?
cards.rule: Retain signed acknowledgments through the present commission and two years afterward. Give the customer a copy when services are rendered.
cards.boundary: The statute includes an Election Code document exception.
cards.mixup: These acknowledgments are distinct from notarization certificates and journal entries.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §3-103(c-5)

cards.title: Itemized fee evidence
cards.front: What records accompany charged services?
cards.rule: Provide itemized receipts and keep fee records. Show notarial fees separately from other charges.
cards.boundary: Ordinary and electronic act ceilings still apply.
cards.mixup: A single unlabeled total obscures the statutory fee evidence.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §3-104(e)

cards.title: Protected notarial data
cards.front: What limits commercial use of journal and recording data?
cards.rule: The Act restricts selling, renting, transferring or otherwise releasing notarial records outside the stated lawful circumstances.
cards.boundary: A qualifying written request may permit a redacted copy of the requested transaction line.
cards.mixup: A broad marketing request is not the limited statutory disclosure.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-104(o)

cards.title: Paper remote and electronic routes
cards.front: Why classify the record before remote service?
cards.rule: Illinois provides remote paper acts under §6-102.5 and electronic acts under Article VI-A. Their workflow and authority requirements differ.
cards.boundary: Electronic acts require the electronic commission and approved system.
cards.mixup: A camera call does not by itself establish either compliant route.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-102.5; Article VI-A; §176.800

cards.title: Physical Illinois venue
cards.front: Where does the electronic notary act?
cards.rule: The notary must be physically within Illinois. The electronic venue is the Illinois jurisdiction of the notary's actual location.
cards.boundary: Abroad principals require the statutory United States connection.
cards.mixup: The signer's remote location does not become the notary's venue.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §§3-105,6A-104(e)-(f)

cards.title: Electronic identity components
cards.front: What supports an unknown electronic principal's identity?
cards.rule: The statutory route combines remote government-credential presentation, front/back credential analysis and dynamic knowledge-based authentication.
cards.boundary: The notary's personal-knowledge route is separately recognized.
cards.mixup: Automated analysis does not eliminate real-time visual comparison.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6A-103(b); §176.835(a)-(b)

cards.title: Dynamic KBA safeguards
cards.front: Which numbers govern this identity assessment?
cards.rule: Use at least five questions with at least five answers each, at least 80% correct and a two-minute limit. One retake within 24 hours replaces at least 40% of questions.
cards.boundary: A second failure bars retry with the same notary within 24 hours. The notary cannot see or record questions or answers.
cards.mixup: These identity metrics are distinct from the 50-question commissioning final.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §176.835(c)

cards.title: Recording duties
cards.front: What survives an unfinished electronic session?
cards.rule: Inform participants before recording. Retain the electronic audio-video recording at least seven years even when the act is not completed.
cards.boundary: The recording is additional to the required journal entry.
cards.mixup: A canceled signature does not automatically authorize deletion.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6A-104(a),(d)

cards.title: Compromised electronic seal
cards.front: What follows discovery of compromise?
cards.rule: Notify appropriate law enforcement, the technology vendor and the Secretary no later than the next business day. Keep seal access under exclusive control.
cards.boundary: An ineffective or insecure device requires stopping electronic acts until the statutory replacement steps are met.
cards.mixup: A coworker's trusted status does not authorize password sharing.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §3-101(c)-(d)

cards.title: Interrupted paper remote act
cards.front: What happens after the remote paper link breaks?
cards.rule: Restart the act from the beginning, including identity confirmation, when the link breaks, a participant exits or the process is compromised.
cards.boundary: The certificate must disclose use of audio-video technology.
cards.mixup: A telephone finish does not cure a broken required session.
cards.source: Illinois Register, June 16, 2023, adopted Part 176 rules — §§176.720,176.730

cards.title: Paper remote return chain
cards.front: What deadlines connect the paper remote signing and return?
cards.rule: The signer sends the entire legible signed document directly to the notary no later than the next day. The notary signs the transmitted copy and returns it within 24 hours after receipt.
cards.boundary: The statute separately addresses an original received with the witnessed copy within 30 days.
cards.mixup: A signature-page-only transmission does not meet the entire-document requirement.
cards.source: Illinois Notary Public Handbook — §6-102.5(c)

commission.summary: Illinois ordinary first applicants complete certified education and the provider's final before applying. Keep education, filing and active authority distinct.

sections.heading: Complete the appropriate certified course
sections.body: The approved course contains at least 180 instructional minutes. Its final has 50 randomized questions from a bank of at least 100, with no more than half true-or-false and a passing score of at least 85%. Retests use different questions. Three failed finals constitute course failure. Apply within two years after passing. A traditional-only course may carry a disclosure that it does not satisfy electronic education.

sections.heading: File and maintain effective authority
sections.body: Residents ordinarily apply online with the specified identification, certificate and bond records. Approved hardship cases may use paper, and qualifying nonresidents use the nonresident paper route. The ordinary bond is $5,000. Remote/electronic work requires the applicable additional coverage. Approval and the official seal precede acting. Resident terms generally last four years and qualifying nonresident terms one year.

sections.heading: Read renewal exceptions and conflicting windows carefully
sections.body: The 2025 rule provides a documented education/exam exception for specified qualifying renewal applicants associated with the legal profession or courts. It is not a blanket first-applicant exception. Online instructions advertise renewal 90 days before expiration, while published Rule 176.350 says 60 days. Confirm the current filing opportunity through the official portal or office. A pending renewal does not extend expired authority.

example.heading: A paralegal's first commission
example.body: A newly hired paralegal has never been commissioned. The law-office employment does not itself establish the renewal-only education exemption. The applicant completes a qualifying certified course and final, then files the resident application with the required documents and waits for approval before obtaining the official seal.

keyFacts: At least 180 instructional minutes describes the course, not a verified uniform examination clock.
The final has 50 randomized questions and requires at least 85%.
A qualifying renewal exemption requires the prescribed signed statement.
The official materials contain a disclosed 60/90-day renewal-window discrepancy.
Expiration ends authority without a grace period.

identification.summary: Illinois requires an authorized identity basis for the person appearing. Appearance, identification and comprehension each need attention.

sections.heading: Select a statutory identity method
sections.body: For an ordinary act, identity may be established through personal knowledge, the oath or affirmation of a credible witness personally known to the notary, or qualifying documentary identification. A document must be valid at the act, issued by a qualifying state agency, federal agency or consulate, and bear a facial photograph and the person's signature. A printed transaction name or unsworn introduction does not supply these methods.

sections.heading: Adapt the lawful procedure to the person
sections.body: A principal physically unable to sign may direct a person other than the notary to sign under Rule 176.610. Both persons appear and are identified, and the required direction statement is placed near the signature. Before taking a blind person's acknowledgment, the notary reads the instrument. For a person who does not speak or understand English, the nature and effect must be translated into an understood language.

example.heading: A client accompanied by a caregiver
example.body: A client cannot physically sign and directs a caregiver to sign. The notary identifies both appearing people under the applicable act's identity rules and records the direction statement near the signature. A caregiver arriving alone with the client's license would not satisfy the principal's required appearance.

keyFacts: Ordinary documentary ID requires both photograph and signature.
The ordinary credible-witness statutory route requires a personally known witness and an oath or affirmation.
Identity documents do not replace personal appearance.
Rule 176.610 requires both the principal and directed signer.
Illinois expressly permits refusal without further explanation.

jurats.summary: Match the actual ceremony to its certificate. Illinois distinguishes acknowledgment, verification upon oath or affirmation, and signature witnessing.

sections.heading: Perform the requested ceremony accurately
sections.body: For acknowledgment, the identified person appears and declares execution for the instrument's purpose. A prior signature may be acknowledged. A representative also declares proper authority and execution as the represented party's act. The verification practice note requires appearance, signing before the notary and an actual oath or affirmation of truth. Signature witnessing requires signing before the notary, with no oath necessary for that form.

sections.heading: Complete and connect the certificate
sections.body: The certificate is signed and dated, identifies the act's jurisdiction and bears the official seal. Its facts describe the actual act. A separate paper certificate is permanently attached in a tamper-evident manner, such as staples. Tape, paper clips and binder clips are excluded. A preferred signature that is not legible or recognizable is accompanied by the legibly printed name immediately adjacent. The official stamp impression is clear, legible and black.

example.heading: Two documents at one appointment
example.body: A tenant brings a previously signed lease for acknowledgment and an unsigned sworn statement for verification. The tenant may acknowledge the earlier lease signature. For the sworn statement, the notary administers the oath or affirmation and observes signing. Each certificate records its own actual ceremony and date.

keyFacts: Acknowledgment can concern a prior signature after required appearance and declaration.
Verification requires the actual oath or affirmation.
Signature witnessing requires the observed signing.
Use the actual act date and jurisdiction.
The ordinary notarial fee ceiling is $5 and the electronic act ceiling is $25.

journals.summary: Contemporaneous journal recording is the default. Illinois has specific law-firm and candidate nomination-document exceptions that must remain visible.

sections.heading: Identify the default and actual exception
sections.body: Record each nonexempt act at notarization. A notary employed by an attorney or law firm has the specific employment-act exception when the employer maintains copies. Journals solely of those employment notarizations belong to the employing attorney or firm, and the rule preserves attorney-client privilege. Specified candidate nomination documents also have a journal exemption. An unrelated commercial instrument does not qualify merely because its signer is a candidate.

sections.heading: Preserve usable records without prohibited identifiers
sections.body: Entries identify the principal, relied-on witnesses and directed signer, document, date, method, fee and physical locations. Do not record prohibited identification numbers, biometrics or electronic signatures of principals and witnesses. Use compliant binding and preprinted numbering for tangible journals, secure recoverable electronic records where used, and ordinary exclusive notary custody. Tangible journals ordinarily remain for seven years after the final recorded act, with the stated governmental-employment retention exception.

example.heading: Law-office and private work
example.body: A firm's employed notary notarizes a retained-copy client instrument during work and later performs a neighbor's private act. The first may fit the law-firm exception. The private act needs the normal journal entry. A journal solely of firm employment acts has the special ownership treatment, so the notary should not collapse both situations into a universal employer-custody rule.

keyFacts: The law-firm exception depends on employment acts and retained document copies.
Specified candidate nomination papers have the separate journal exemption.
Government ID numbers and biometric identifiers are prohibited journal entries.
Record no charge explicitly and itemize clerical charges separately.
Notify the Secretary within 10 business days after discovering a lost, stolen or compromised journal.

prohibited-acts.summary: The commission authorizes defined notarial acts. It does not remove conflicts, authorize blank certificates or grant general legal-practice authority.

sections.heading: Screen the transaction before signing
sections.body: Do not notarize your own signature, including a corporate signature. Do not acknowledge an instrument in which your name appears as a transaction party. Do not sign blank affidavits or acknowledgment certificates, act during suspension or revocation, or change a written instrument after anyone has signed it. A regular commission does not permit representing yourself as an electronic notary without that separate commission.

sections.heading: Keep services, advertising and records within authority
sections.body: The Act restricts preparing legal instruments and explaining or certifying contents, while preserving its stated attorney-notary provisions. Covered non-English advertising requires the prescribed bilingual nonattorney notice, posting and signed acknowledgment procedures. Itemize charged services and keep records. Protect notarial records from unauthorized third-party disclosure or commercial sale. The limited redacted-line-item request procedure does not make the entire journal a marketing resource.

example.heading: A real-estate office request
example.body: A supervisor asks the notary to edit a signed deed, sign several blank acknowledgments for the next week and lend the stamp during vacation. Each request crosses a separate Illinois limit. The notary preserves the instrument, refuses advance certification and keeps the seal secure while performing only properly presented lawful acts.

keyFacts: Self-notarization remains prohibited in corporate capacity.
Being named as a party bars acknowledgment of that instrument.
Do not sign blank certificates or alter signed instruments.
A private waiver does not expand legal-drafting authority.
Covered non-English advertising has specific notice and record duties.

electronic-ron.summary: Illinois remote paper acts and electronic acts follow distinct statutory routes. Electronic authority, identity technology and record retention must match the procedure.

sections.heading: Classify and authorize the act
sections.body: Remote paper work falls under §6-102.5 and related rules. Electronic notarization falls under Article VI-A and requires the electronic commission and approved system. The electronic notary is physically in Illinois and uses the actual Illinois jurisdiction as venue. Electronic principals abroad need the statutory United States filing, matter, property or transaction connection. Required audio-video communication is live and simultaneous.

sections.heading: Secure identity and the electronic record
sections.body: For the electronic statutory documentary route, remote credential presentation is combined with credential analysis and dynamic KBA. KBA has at least five questions with five choices each, at least 80% correct and a two-minute limit, with restricted retakes. The notary cannot see or record the KBA questions or answers. Inform participants of recording and retain the electronic recording at least seven years even if the act is not completed. Keep electronic seal access exclusive and report compromise to the specified recipients by the next business day.

sections.heading: Follow paper remote transmission rules
sections.body: For the paper remote procedure, the signer sends the entire legible signed document directly to the notary by no later than the next day. The notary signs and returns the transmitted copy within 24 hours after receipt. The certificate discloses audio-video use. Rule 176.720 requires restarting the act after the link breaks, a participant exits or the procedure is compromised.

example.heading: A remote session interrupted at signing
example.body: During a paper remote act the video link disconnects. The notary restarts the procedure from the beginning, including identity, after a compliant connection is established. The signer then sends the entire signed instrument within the statutory next-day limit, and the notary performs the required return step and remote certificate statement.

keyFacts: An electronic commission and approved system are required for electronic acts.
The electronic notary must physically be in Illinois.
Electronic audio-video recordings remain at least seven years even after noncompletion.
KBA identity metrics differ from the commissioning examination.
A compromised electronic seal triggers next-business-day reporting.

articles.keyword: Illinois law firm notary journal exception
articles.title: Illinois Law-Firm Journals and Retained Document Copies
articles.description: Apply the law-firm journal exception to office work, outside acts, ownership and privileged records.
articles.lede: A legal office's document files can change the journal analysis for its employed notary. The specific rule has conditions that should be checked transaction by transaction.

sections.heading: Start with the actual employment act
sections.body: Rule 176.900(f) addresses a notary employed by an attorney or law firm and notarizations performed during that employment. It requires the attorney or firm to maintain copies of the notarized documents. Consider a litigation assistant notarizing a client's retained-copy affidavit during assigned office work. Those facts support the specific exception. Merely working in the same building as a lawyer would not establish the required employment relationship or copy retention.

sections.heading: Keep outside appointments in view
sections.body: The assistant later notarizes a neighbor's unrelated private document at home. The firm's client files do not preserve that instrument, and the act is outside the described employment. The general contemporaneous journal requirement therefore needs its own analysis. The notary should identify whether each transaction actually satisfies the exception before omitting an entry, even when the same stamp and commission are used for both office and private service.

sections.heading: Apply the specific ownership provision
sections.body: The rule expressly assigns journals of notarizations performed solely within the course of employment with an attorney or firm to that employing attorney or firm. That specific provision matters alongside the Act's ordinary employer-custody rules. A journal containing only qualifying office acts presents a different set of stated facts from a mixed personal-and-business journal. The word solely should be preserved when explaining the rule or arranging record custody.

sections.heading: Preserve privilege during inspection
sections.body: The law-firm provision also says an attorney or firm need not violate attorney-client privilege by allowing or authorizing inspection of notarizations recorded in a journal. A request for records should therefore be assessed under both the journal provisions and the applicable privilege protection. The exception does not authorize a notary to sell client information or release every office file. Illinois separately restricts third-party use of journal contents and associated notarial records.

faqs.q: Does every act by a law-office employee qualify?
faqs.a: The specific exception concerns employment notarizations for which the employing attorney or firm maintains document copies.

faqs.q: Who owns a journal solely of those employment acts?
faqs.a: Rule 176.900(f) makes it the property of the employing attorney or law firm.

articles.keyword: Illinois candidate nominating petition notary journal
articles.title: Illinois Candidate Papers and the Journal Exemption
articles.description: Identify the listed candidate nomination documents and preserve the other notarial steps.
articles.h1: Journaling Candidate Nomination Documents in Illinois
articles.lede: The candidate-document exception is defined by the document and its filing purpose. A candidate's unrelated paperwork still needs ordinary analysis.

sections.heading: Identify the document on the list
sections.body: Rule 176.900(g) and Act §3-107(f) identify nominating petitions, petitions of candidacy, petitions for nomination, nominating papers and nomination papers associated with a candidate for public office. Suppose a campaign volunteer brings a qualifying nomination petition for filing on the candidate's behalf. The notary should identify the instrument accurately before relying on this exception. The exemption is tied to the specified electoral documents and candidate filing relationship.

sections.heading: Preserve the actual notarization
sections.body: The provision concerns keeping or recording the act in a journal. The signer still participates in the notarial act, and the notary still establishes identity and performs the ceremony the certificate describes. A petition affidavit requiring verification calls for the oath or affirmation and the required signing procedure. The journal exception supplies no authority to certify an absent person's statement, skip identification or sign blank certificates for later campaign use.

sections.heading: Read the historical protection accurately
sections.body: Rule 176.900(h) states that the listed exemption applies to acts performed before, on or after the amendment's effective date. It also says the specified failure to keep or record such an act does not affect the act's validity and is not an Act violation. This addresses a particular journal omission. A reviewer should preserve that scope when discussing an older nomination paper instead of treating every missing historical journal entry as automatically fatal.

sections.heading: Screen unrelated candidate business
sections.body: The same candidate might ask the notary to acknowledge a private equipment lease for the candidate's business. A commercial lease does not become a listed nomination paper because the signer is running for office or because the appointment occurs during campaign season. The notary returns to the ordinary journal analysis for that transaction. Maintaining this document-specific distinction prevents the election exception from swallowing record duties for a candidate's everyday commercial affairs.

faqs.q: Does candidate status exempt every notarization?
faqs.a: No. The journal exception identifies particular candidate nomination documents.

faqs.q: Does the exception remove the oath for a petition affidavit?
faqs.a: The journal exception does not remove the requirements of the actual notarial act.

articles.intent: Protect journal privacy and handle requests
articles.title: Illinois Journal Privacy from Entry to Disclosure
articles.description: Record required transaction facts, avoid prohibited identifiers and limit requested copies.
articles.h1: Protecting an Illinois Notary Journal's Information
articles.lede: A useful journal records the act without accumulating prohibited identity data. Illinois controls both what goes into the record and how information leaves it.

sections.heading: Capture the required transaction
sections.body: Rule 176.910 requires the principal's name, relied-on credible witnesses, any directed signer, document title or description, date, method, fee and physical locations of notary and principal. For entry purposes, address means city and state only. Consider an office that buys a generic multistate journal. Its template should be evaluated against these Illinois requirements before use, because a printed box does not make every requested data item lawful or necessary.

sections.heading: Leave prohibited identifiers out
sections.body: The same rule excludes government-assigned identification numbers, other numbers identifying the principal, biometric identifiers and specified linked personal information. It also excludes the principal's and witnesses' electronic signatures from the journal. An employee who believes that a driver's-license number and fingerprint would make the record stronger must respect these limits. The signed electronic instrument and the journal are separate records with different content requirements.

sections.heading: Redact an accidental entry before access
sections.body: If prohibited information is inadvertently recorded, Rule 176.910(d) requires redaction before public access or copies are provided. The correction should serve the privacy duty while preserving the integrity of the transaction history. Electronic-journal rules recognize required privacy redaction while otherwise protecting content and sequence against alteration or deletion. A request for a copy should trigger a review of the information actually disclosed, including any sensitive data entered by mistake.

sections.heading: Use the limited disclosure mechanism
sections.body: Act §6-104(o) restricts commercial sale and third-party availability of journal contents, recordings and associated records outside the specified lawful circumstances. It permits a transaction-specific line-item copy upon a written request identifying parties, document type and month and year, after personal identifying information is redacted. A marketing company's request for every client entry is a different proposal. The statutory line-item mechanism does not authorize release of the entire unredacted journal.

faqs.q: May a notary record a driver's-license number because a template asks for it?
faqs.a: Rule 176.910(c) prohibits the government identification number in the journal.

faqs.q: May a qualifying requester automatically receive the whole journal?
faqs.a: The stated request procedure concerns a redacted copy of the requested transaction line item.

articles.keyword: Illinois notary physically unable to sign
articles.title: Directed Signatures and Accessible Illinois Acknowledgments
articles.description: Work through physical inability, blind signers and language comprehension under Illinois rules.
articles.h1: Adapting the Illinois Ceremony to the Signer
articles.lede: A person's physical or communication needs change the preparation for an appointment. The principal's lawful participation and the notary's accurate certificate remain central.

sections.heading: Establish direction and both participants
sections.body: Rule 176.610 addresses a person physically unable to sign who directs someone other than the notary to sign the person's name. Both the principal and directed signer appear and are identified under the applicable identity provisions at signing. Imagine a client with a hand injury who brings a caregiver. The notary must establish the client's direction and identify both people. The caregiver arriving alone with the client's license would leave the principal's required appearance unsatisfied.

sections.heading: Document who affixed the signature
sections.body: The rule requires the prescribed or substantially similar statement near the signature identifying the individual who signed and the person at whose direction it was affixed. This communicates the execution procedure to someone later reading the document. The helper's occupational title by itself would not describe who directed the signature. The journal rule also calls for the name of another person who signed for the principal where the act is subject to journal recording.

sections.heading: Read the instrument before a blind person's acknowledgment
sections.body: Act §6-104(e) specifically requires reading the instrument to a blind person before taking that person's acknowledgment. This statutory step should be included in appointment planning so that the notary has time to perform it. The acknowledgment still requires the appearing person's identity and declaration of execution. A preprinted waiver or a companion's reassurance does not replace the reading specified by the Illinois Act for this acknowledgment.

sections.heading: Address understanding before acknowledgment
sections.body: Under §6-104(f), a person who does not speak or understand English must receive translation of the instrument's nature and effect into a language the person understands before acknowledgment. This is distinct from deciding which identity credential qualifies. A consular credential may support identity when it meets the statutory requirements, but the credential itself does not demonstrate understanding of the instrument's nature and effect. Evaluate both requirements on the facts presented.

faqs.q: Can the notary be the directed signer under Rule 176.610?
faqs.a: The rule describes a directed person other than the notary.

faqs.q: Does a caregiver's appearance replace the principal's appearance?
faqs.a: Both the principal and the directed signer must appear and be identified under the rule.

articles.intent: Distinguish notarial ceremonies in a mixed packet
articles.title: Three Illinois Ceremonies in One Appointment
articles.description: Distinguish prior-signature acknowledgment, sworn verification and signature witnessing.
articles.h1: Choosing the Ceremony Described by the Certificate
articles.lede: A packet may contain several certificate types. Perform and document each required event accurately instead of using one routine for every page.

sections.heading: Acknowledge an earlier signature
sections.body: An apartment manager brings a lease already signed by a tenant who is now present. The acknowledgment practice note permits the identified signer to acknowledge the existing signature as their own. The signer declares execution for the purpose stated in the instrument. The prior signature does not eliminate appearance, identification or the declaration. The notary's certificate records today's acknowledgment rather than falsely stating that the earlier signing was personally witnessed.

sections.heading: Administer the sworn truth declaration
sections.body: The tenant also brings an unsigned affidavit requesting verification upon oath or affirmation. The handbook's verification practice note requires the person to appear and sign before the notary, with the notary administering the oath or affirmation. A printed statement saying the document was sworn does not perform that ceremony by itself. A signer who prefers a solemn affirmation may use that authorized alternative, with the actual truth declaration occurring before completion.

sections.heading: Observe signature witnessing
sections.body: A third page requests signature witnessing without an oath. Its practice note requires the identified person to appear and sign before the notary. An already signed page cannot be treated as though its signing was observed merely because the customer acknowledges it informally. The requested certificate describes an actual witnessed event. If the necessary event has not occurred, the notary must avoid signing a certificate that states otherwise.

sections.heading: Match the certificate and representative facts
sections.body: A corporate officer in the same appointment may acknowledge on behalf of an entity. The representative definition includes proper authority and execution as the represented entity's act. The representative form records the capacity and represented party. Every certificate must carry its actual act date, jurisdiction, official signature and seal. Accurate matching of ceremony, person and capacity prevents a stack of papers from turning distinct declarations into a single undocumented assumption.

faqs.q: Can an acknowledgment concern a signature made earlier?
faqs.a: Yes, the signer must appear, be identified and acknowledge the signature under the handbook procedure.

faqs.q: Does signature witnessing automatically require an oath?
faqs.a: The handbook states that an oath is not necessary for that form, while signing before the notary is required.

articles.title: Keeping an Illinois Paper Certificate Connected and Readable
articles.description: Use permanent attachment, truthful venue and date, legible signatures and a compliant seal.
articles.lede: A separate certificate can travel farther than the appointment itself. Its physical connection and readable official details help preserve what the notary actually did.

sections.heading: Use a permanent connection
sections.body: Rule 176.600(c) requires a paper certificate to be permanently and securely attached to its document in a tamper-evident manner. Staples are among the listed methods. Tape, paper clips and binder clips are expressly excluded. Consider a closing office that wants every certificate loosely clipped for later packet assembly. The notary should arrange a compliant permanent connection to the specific instrument whose act is being certified, preserving the relationship between record and certificate.

sections.heading: State the actual act facts
sections.body: Section 6-103 requires a signed and dated certificate identifying the jurisdiction where the act is performed. A document prepared in Chicago can be notarized elsewhere in Illinois, with the actual act location supplying the venue. The contract's drafting date does not automatically become the notarial date. These fields describe the notary's event. They should be completed from the appointment facts rather than copied mechanically from a cover letter or the instrument's opening paragraph.

sections.heading: Make the official signature recognizable
sections.body: The notary uses the commissioned name or initials required by §6-104(a). Rule 176.600(d) adds a readability safeguard when the notary's preferred handwritten signature is not legible or recognizable. In that case, the notary also prints the name legibly immediately adjacent to the signature. The printed name supports the official handwritten execution. It does not authorize another employee to sign for the notary or replace the required signature with an unrelated business title.

sections.heading: Check the seal as information
sections.body: The ordinary official seal uses the statutory rectangular format and required wording, including the commissioned name and expiration date. The border may not exceed one inch in height by two and one-half inches in length. Section 6-103(c) requires a clear, legible black-ink impression capable of photographic reproduction. A beautiful impression with the wrong commission information still needs correction, and an employer's stamp-design preference does not change the legal specifications.

faqs.q: Can a binder clip permanently attach a separate certificate?
faqs.a: Rule 176.600(c) expressly excludes binder clips.

faqs.q: What accompanies an illegible preferred signature?
faqs.a: The rule requires the notary's legibly printed name immediately adjacent to the signature.

articles.intent: Apply covered advertising and acknowledgment duties
articles.title: Illinois Non-English Advertising and Customer Disclosures
articles.description: Understand notices, fee posting, signed acknowledgments and record retention for covered advertising.
articles.h1: Disclosures for Covered Illinois Notary Advertising
articles.lede: Advertising in another language can create several connected disclosure duties. The Act's conditions and exceptions should be checked before publishing and before service.

sections.heading: Describe the actual professional role
sections.body: Section 3-103 addresses covered notaries who are not attorneys or accredited immigration representatives and advertise in a language other than English. It requires a conspicuous notice in English and the advertising language describing the lack of Illinois attorney status and the limits on legal drafting and advice. Imagine a notary publishing a Spanish-language service page. The description must reflect actual qualifications and must avoid the prohibited literal title translation that implies lawyer-like authority, including the statute's example of notario.

sections.heading: Connect the advertisement to the fee posting
sections.body: For covered notaries, §3-103(b) requires the lawful fee schedule to be prominently posted at the recorded place of business in English and the language used to solicit services. It also addresses the disavowal of legal representation. A receptionist's oral price quote does not itself supply this posted schedule. The notary should ensure that the public-facing information at the business matches the language and services actually advertised and preserves the required disclosures.

sections.heading: Obtain the signed customer acknowledgment
sections.body: Section 3-103(c-5) generally requires the covered notary to provide the stated written nonattorney acknowledgment in English and the advertising language before rendering services. The recipient signs it before service and receives a copy when service is rendered. The statute includes an exception for the specified Election Code-related documents. This customer acknowledgment is a separate disclosure record. It should not be confused with the legal act of acknowledging a document signature.

sections.heading: Retain disclosures and itemize charges
sections.body: The signed customer acknowledgments remain through the notary's present commission and for two years afterward. Separately, §3-104(e) requires itemized receipts and fee records, with notarial fees shown apart from other assessed charges. An office can therefore have several different records associated with one appointment, each serving its own statutory purpose. A generic receipt does not replace the signed disclosure, and the disclosure does not authorize legal advice beyond independently held qualifications.

faqs.q: Is the signed nonattorney acknowledgment the same as a notarization certificate?
faqs.a: No. It is the separate customer disclosure record required for the covered advertising circumstances.

faqs.q: How long are signed covered acknowledgments retained?
faqs.a: Through the present commission and for two years afterward under §3-103(c-5).

articles.keyword: Illinois remote paper notarization next day
articles.intent: Follow the remote paper transmission chain
articles.title: The Illinois Remote Paper Document Chain
articles.description: Track the live ceremony, interrupted sessions, complete transmission and timely notary return.
articles.h1: Following a Remote Paper Instrument from Camera to Return
articles.lede: Illinois's paper remote procedure combines a live ceremony with a document-transmission chain. Both parts need to be completed under their own rules.

sections.heading: Establish the authorized live procedure
sections.body: Section 6-102.5 and Rules 176.700 through 176.730 govern the remote paper route. The notary confirms identity using the authorized means and the communication permits real-time seeing and speaking with adequate clarity. The procedure must connect the record presented for the act with the record on which the principal signs or makes a statement. An ordinary recorded clip or voice-only call does not supply the described live audio-video procedure.

sections.heading: Restart after a broken link
sections.body: Rule 176.720 requires restarting from the beginning, including identity confirmation, when a participant exits the session, the audio-video link breaks or the process is compromised. Consider a signer whose connection fails just as the signature is being made. Continuing from a frozen image and later text message would bypass the restart rule. Once a compliant session is available, the notary repeats the required process instead of assuming that the earlier partial observation completed the act.

sections.heading: Receive the whole signed document
sections.body: The signer must send a legible copy of the entire signed document directly to the notary by overnight mail, fax or electronic means no later than the day after signing. This rule concerns both timing and completeness. A signature-page photograph sent two days later misses more than one part of the statutory chain. Planning the transmission method before the appointment helps the principal send the actual complete instrument that corresponds to the live session.

sections.heading: Return and describe the completed act
sections.body: The notary signs the transmitted copy as witness and returns it through a permitted means within 24 hours after receipt. Section 6-102.5(c)(3) separately addresses an original received with the witnessed copy within 30 days and its permitted execution treatment. Rule 176.730 requires the remote certificate's audio-video statement. The certificate therefore records the actual remote method while the document chain preserves the connection between the observed signing and returned notarial record.

faqs.q: Is sending only the signature page enough?
faqs.a: The statute requires a legible copy of the entire signed document.

faqs.q: When must the notary return the transmitted copy?
faqs.a: Within 24 hours after receipt, following the required signing step.

articles.title: Illinois Electronic Identity Checks Beyond a Video Image
articles.description: Study credential analysis, real-time comparison and dynamic KBA without confusing commissioning exam rules.
articles.h1: Electronic Identity Verification for an Illinois Remote Principal
articles.lede: The commissioning final and the principal's dynamic identity assessment serve different purposes. Their numbers and participants should be kept distinct.

sections.heading: Build the documentary identity chain
sections.body: For the statutory electronic route where personal knowledge is not used, §6A-103(b)(2) combines remote presentation of a government credential, front-and-back credential analysis and dynamic knowledge-based authentication. Rule 176.835 describes third-party analysis and the notary's real-time visual comparison of credential and principal. A successful automated result is a component of the procedure. The notary still needs to see whether the appearing person and credential are consistent.

sections.heading: Apply the dynamic quiz requirements
sections.body: Rule 176.835(c) requires at least five questions derived from the principal's personal history or identity, at least five answer choices per question, at least 80% correct and completion within two minutes. These are identity-proofing metrics for the remote principal. They differ from the certified commissioning final's 50 questions and 85% passing score. A learner should identify which assessment is being discussed before applying any numerical specification.

sections.heading: Respect the retake boundaries
sections.body: After the first failed dynamic quiz, the principal may take one retest within 24 hours. At least 40% of the earlier questions must be replaced. After the second failure, the principal may not retry with the same electronic notary within 24 hours of that failure. A vendor screen offering unlimited immediate tries would need correction to comply with these limits. Paying another service charge does not waive the statutory and regulatory identity procedure.

sections.heading: Preserve independent answers and workflow integrity
sections.body: The notary must not be able to see or record the KBA questions or answers. Coaching a principal through displayed answers would undermine this required separation of access. Rule 176.825(c) also requires restarting identity verification if the individual exits the workflow before completing it. A compliant system therefore needs both protected assessment information and a process that recognizes interrupted verification instead of silently resuming at an unverified final step.

faqs.q: May the notary read the KBA questions to help the principal?
faqs.a: Rule 176.835(c)(8) requires that the notary not be able to see or record the questions or answers.

faqs.q: Is 85% the dynamic KBA passing score?
faqs.a: The dynamic KBA rule requires at least 80%. The 85% figure belongs to the commissioning final.

articles.intent: Preserve electronic records and respond to compromise
articles.title: Illinois Electronic Records After the Session Ends
articles.description: Maintain recordings, protect exclusive seal access and respond to compromised credentials.
articles.h1: Preserving the Illinois Electronic Notarial Record
articles.lede: The electronic appointment creates records and security duties that continue after the video closes. An unfinished act can still leave a recording that must be retained.

sections.heading: Make the record verifiable
sections.body: The electronic signature and seal must be attached or logically associated with the electronic certificate in a manner capable of independent verification and rendering later modification evident. A simple editable image does not establish these safeguards. The electronic certificate also identifies the act's jurisdiction and the audio-video method where used. The notary must be physically within Illinois, with the actual Illinois jurisdiction of the notary's location supplying the venue.

sections.heading: Explain and retain the recording
sections.body: Before the electronic audio-video act, the notary informs participating persons that it will be recorded. The recording is additional to the journal entry. Under §6A-104(d), it remains for at least seven years regardless of whether the act was completed. Suppose the principal withdraws before the electronic seal is affixed. That noncompletion does not by itself permit immediate deletion of the recording already created under the statutory procedure.

sections.heading: Protect exclusive access
sections.body: The electronic signature and seal remain under the notary's exclusive control. Another employee cannot use them to cover an appointment, even if experienced with the platform. Rule 176.815 requires protected authentication, and the Act restricts disclosure of access information. Secure journal backups and protections against unauthorized access also continue beyond the live session. Employer ownership of a computer does not turn the notary's seal credential into a shared office login.

sections.heading: Respond to a compromised seal
sections.body: Section 3-101(d)(2) requires notice to appropriate law enforcement, the technology vendor and the Secretary no later than the next business day after theft, compromise or vandalism of the electronic signature or seal. Section 3-101(c) requires stopping electronic acts when the device or technology is ineffective or insecure until the specified replacement and notice steps are completed. A suspected exposure should therefore be handled as a security event with the actual statutory recipients and timing.

faqs.q: Can an unfinished electronic act's recording be deleted immediately?
faqs.a: Section 6A-104(d) requires at least seven years of retention regardless of completion.

faqs.q: Who must receive notice of a compromised electronic seal?
faqs.a: Appropriate law enforcement, the technology vendor and the Secretary, no later than the next business day.
